source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Aurora campus publishes 114 megawatts of IT capacity across three buildings, the largest disclosed power figure in Illinois and 48 percent of the state's disclosed total.

The campus covers 450,000 square feet, which works out to about 6.3 megawatts per 10,000 square feet. That ratio is typical for hyperscale colocation built in the last decade, so the site's weight comes from its size rather than any unusual density. At 40 kilowatts per rack, a common AI training density, 114 megawatts supports roughly 2,850 racks. Illinois has 44 mapped data center facilities and only six publish a power figure at all, so one campus accounts for nearly half of what the state discloses.

For AI, the megawatt figure is the one that matters. IT capacity bounds how many accelerators a building can hold, and 114 megawatts is the largest such budget published in Illinois. The density figure is the caution. A campus at 6.3 megawatts per 10,000 square feet is laid out for conventional colocation, and the operator publishes nothing about cooling technology or cooling source, so nothing here shows the halls can sustain the thermal load of a dense accelerator cluster.

What the record omits is substantial. There is no total campus power draw, no PUE, no renewable sourcing, no power delivery tier or redundancy topology, and no interconnect uplinks to cloud regions. Whether Aurora's 114 megawatts is capped by the local grid, and whether the site can move training traffic onto the cloud backbone, are precisely the questions the grid constraint turns on, and none of them are answered here. Green Globes is the only environmental fact disclosed.
